title: Factors to Consider Before Training
description: Pre-training essentials: PAR-Q, SMART goals, current fitness, age, lifestyle, cost and available facilities.
content_html:
Why Planning Ahead Matters

Before a coach writes a single session plan, they must gather information about the performer they are working with. Jumping straight into training without this groundwork is ineffective at best and dangerous at worst. A training programme that ignores a performer's medical history, current fitness level, lifestyle or available resources will fail to produce results — and may even cause harm. The factors to consider fall into two broad groups: personal factors (relating to the individual) and environmental factors (relating to the setting and resources available).

Health Screening and the PAR-Q

The first step in any new training programme is a PAR-Q (Physical Activity Readiness Questionnaire). This is a short questionnaire that asks about symptoms such as chest pain, dizziness, bone or joint problems, and whether a doctor has ever advised against vigorous exercise. A 'yes' answer to any question does not automatically prevent someone from training, but it flags that medical clearance should be sought before they begin. The PAR-Q protects both the performer and the coach: if a participant suffers an adverse event during training and no health screening was completed, the coach may face professional or legal consequences. Health screening more broadly includes checking for medical conditions such as asthma, diabetes or a known heart condition, each of which will influence the type, intensity and duration of training that is appropriate.

Key Fact

The PAR-Q is completed before starting any new training programme. It screens for medical conditions and cardiovascular risk factors. A 'yes' answer means the performer should seek medical advice before training begins.

Current Fitness Level and Test Results

Once health screening is complete, the coach needs to establish a baseline — a starting point from which progress can be measured. This means carrying out appropriate fitness tests (such as the multi-stage fitness test for cardiovascular endurance or the sit-and-reach for flexibility) and recording the results. Knowing the performer's current fitness level allows the coach to set training at an appropriate intensity — too easy and no adaptation will occur; too hard and the performer risks injury or drop-out. Test results also highlight specific strengths and weaknesses, so the programme can target the components of fitness most relevant to the performer's sport.

Goals and SMART Targets

Understanding what the performer wants to achieve is essential before any programme is written. Goals should be set using the SMART framework: Specific (clearly defined, e.g. 'improve 10 km run time'), Measurable (tracked with a number or test result), Agreed/Achievable (agreed between coach and performer, and within reach), Realistic (attainable given the performer's current level and resources) and Time-phased (with a clear deadline). SMART targets improve exercise adherence — performers who have a clear goal are more motivated and more likely to stick to the programme. Setting both short-term targets (e.g. improve press-up score by 10 in six weeks) and a longer-term goal (e.g. complete a 10 km race in under 50 minutes by the end of term) helps maintain focus and momentum throughout training.

Personal Factors: Age, Gender, Lifestyle and Time Available

Beyond health and goals, the coach must consider a range of personal factors. Age affects the type of training that is safe and effective: younger athletes with developing bodies may need to avoid heavy resistance work, while older performers have reduced muscle elasticity and need more recovery time between sessions. Gender influences physiological differences in average strength, hormonal profile and some injury susceptibilities, and should inform exercise selection and intensity guidance. Lifestyle — covering factors such as diet, sleep patterns, work or school commitments, stress levels and social habits — determines how much the performer can recover between sessions. A performer who sleeps poorly, eats erratically and has a physically demanding job will need a lighter training load than someone with a healthy routine and plenty of rest. Time available for training and the cost of training are practical limits: the programme must be realistic about how many sessions per week a performer can commit to, and what resources they can afford.

Key Fact

Personal factors include health, fitness, age, gender, lifestyle, time available for training and cost of training. Each one can limit or shape what a training programme looks like in practice.

Environmental Factors: Facilities, Equipment and the Sport's Demands

Even a perfectly designed programme is useless if the performer cannot access the facilities or equipment needed to carry it out. Environmental factors include the availability of a swimming pool, gym, track, sports hall or open space, and the equipment (resistance machines, free weights, agility ladders, etc.) that the performer can use. The coach must also analyse the demands of the sport: a swimmer needs cardiovascular endurance and muscular endurance training, whereas a sprinter needs power, speed and explosive strength work. Designing a programme without analysing what the sport actually requires means training the wrong components.

Safety, Injury Risk and Warm-Up/Cool-Down

Safety must be considered at every stage of programme design. Before training begins, the coach should carry out a risk assessment — checking facilities, equipment, participant numbers and the environment for hazards. A performer with a known vulnerability (a previous knee injury, for example) needs a programme that avoids aggravating that area. Warm-up and cool-down must be built into every session: a warm-up raises heart rate and temperature, increases blood flow to muscles and reduces injury risk, while a cool-down gradually lowers heart rate, removes metabolic waste products from working muscles and aids recovery. Skipping these components significantly increases both acute and overuse injury risk.

A risk assessment before a training session involves four key checks: facilities (are surfaces safe, is space adequate, is the venue free from trip hazards?), equipment (is it in good repair, correctly adjusted and appropriate for the participants?), participants (are there any medical conditions, previous injuries or fitness concerns that change what is safe for this group?) and rules or laws (does the activity comply with health and safety regulations and the sport's governing body guidelines?). A written risk assessment protects participants and demonstrates the coach's duty of care. Even for informal training sessions, mentally running through these checks before starting is good professional practice.

A training programme that a performer cannot sustain financially or logistically will fail, regardless of its scientific soundness. If a coach prescribes five gym sessions per week but the performer can only afford two visits and has school commitments every evening, adherence will collapse. Cost of training covers gym membership fees, equipment purchases, travel, specialist coaching and competition entry fees. Time available must account for school or work, family responsibilities, travel to training venues and recovery time. The best coaches design programmes that fit the performer's real life — not an idealised schedule. A realistic but consistent programme will always outperform a perfect programme that is abandoned after two weeks.
exam_tip_html: In short-answer questions, the examiner will often give you a scenario — for example, a 16-year-old with asthma who wants to get fitter for football but can only train twice a week at school. Your job is to identify and apply the relevant factors. Name each factor precisely (use the correct terms — 'personal factors', 'PAR-Q', 'SMART targets', 'environmental factors'), then explain why it matters for that specific performer. In extended-answer questions worth 6 or 8 marks, show that factors interact: for instance, the performer's age and medical condition (asthma) together limit the intensity that is safe, which must then be reflected in the SMART target that is set. Answers that treat each factor in isolation typically fall in the Developing band; answers that show how factors connect reach Mastering.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Before designing a training programme, a coach must consider personal factors (health, fitness, age, gender, lifestyle, time available and cost) and environmental factors (facilities and equipment available).
  • The PAR-Q is a health screening questionnaire completed before any new programme begins; a 'yes' answer means the performer should seek medical advice first.
  • Goals must be set using the SMART framework (Specific, Measurable, Agreed/Achievable, Realistic, Time-phased) to improve motivation and exercise adherence.
  • Safety considerations include a risk assessment, knowledge of injury history and medical conditions, and building warm-up and cool-down into every session.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a personal factor that must be considered before designing a training programme?
A) The quality of the gym equipment
B) The performer's lifestyle
C) The size of the sports hall
D) The weather on training days
State two personal factors a coach must consider before starting a training programme with a new performer.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: health / fitness / age / gender / lifestyle / time available for training / cost of training. Answers that list the same factor twice score only 1 mark. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why completing a PAR-Q is important before a new performer starts a training programme.
practice_questions.marks: A simple point scores 1 mark (e.g. 'it checks for health issues'). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. 'it identifies medical conditions such as a heart problem that could make vigorous exercise dangerous, allowing the coach to seek medical clearance first'). A further developed point or a second distinct reason scores 3 marks (e.g. add 'it also protects the coach professionally — if a performer has a health event during training and no screening was completed, the coach may be liable'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A coach is designing a training programme for a 45-year-old recreational tennis player who has a part-time job and can only train three times per week.

Describe two factors the coach should consider before writing the programme.
practice_questions.marks: Two marks available per factor (1 for identifying the factor, 1 for explaining its relevance to this specific performer). For example: age (1) — at 45 the performer will have reduced muscle elasticity and require more recovery time between sessions, so the programme must include adequate rest days (1); time available (1) — only three sessions per week limits total training volume, so each session must be well-targeted at the components most relevant to tennis (1). Accept any two relevant factors with applied explanation. [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A 16-year-old student wants to improve her performance in the 800 m. She has mild asthma and attends school five days a week. She can train four evenings per week at a local running track and has access to a school gym.

Discuss the factors a coach should consider before designing a training programme for this performer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A thorough discussion covering personal factors (medical condition — asthma affects safe exercise intensity and may require an inhaler protocol; age — growing body, appropriate resistance loading; time available — four evenings, realistic volume; current fitness level — baseline testing needed) and environmental factors (running track and school gym — enables both cardiovascular and strength work). SMART goal-setting referenced: e.g. 'improve 800 m time from 3:20 to 3:05 by the end of term' shows all five criteria. Interaction between factors noted — e.g. asthma and intensity constraints must be reflected in the measurable and realistic elements of the SMART target.
Secure (3-4 marks): At least three factors identified with some explanation and partial application to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): Two factors identified but explanation is superficial.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A newly qualified coach is planning a training programme for a group of adult beginners at a local leisure centre. The group includes participants aged 18-55, one of whom has recently had a knee operation and another who is a smoker with high blood pressure.

Evaluate how effectively the coach can design a safe and appropriate training programme given the range of personal and environmental factors present in this scenario.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Evaluates both the breadth of personal factors (wide age range requires differentiated intensity; medical conditions — post-surgery knee and high blood pressure — demand PAR-Q completion and possible medical clearance before these individuals train; lifestyle factor of smoking reduces cardiovascular efficiency) and environmental factors (leisure centre likely provides good facilities, but coach must check equipment suitability and space for the group size). SMART goals must be set individually within the group context. The challenge of designing one programme that meets all needs is weighed against the option of sub-grouping. A substantiated judgement is given — e.g. the coach can design a safe programme but must conduct individual health screening, set differentiated targets and build a thorough risk assessment into every session; the wide variance in personal factors makes a single-plan approach insufficient.
Secure (5-6 marks): Multiple personal and environmental factors identified and applied to the scenario; an attempt at evaluative judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant factors listed with some explanation; limited evaluation.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points with no evaluation. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which one of the following correctly describes what the PAR-Q is used for?
options: To measure a performer's current cardiovascular endurance before testing
To screen for medical conditions and health risks before starting a training programme
To record a performer's SMART targets at the start of a programme
To assess the quality of the training facilities available to the performer

knowledge_checks.q: Which one of the following is an environmental factor a coach must consider before designing a training programme?
The 'R' in the SMART goal-setting framework stands for _____, meaning the goal must be achievable given the performer's current level, available time and resources.
A coach builds a _____ into every session to raise heart rate, increase blood flow to muscles and reduce the risk of injury before the main training begins.
Match each factor to the correct category.
right: Personal factor — relates to the individual performer's body or health
Environmental factor — relates to the training setting and resources
Personal factor — relates to the performer's schedule and lifestyle commitments

flashcard_questions.a: Physical Activity Readiness Questionnaire — a health screening tool completed before starting a new training programme.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is a PAR-Q completed before training begins?
flashcard_questions.a: To identify medical conditions or risk factors that could make exercise unsafe for the performer.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the five letters of the SMART goal-setting framework.
What are the seven personal factors listed for pre-training consideration?
flashcard_questions.a: Health, fitness, age, gender, lifestyle, time available for training, and cost of training.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the two environmental factors a coach must consider before writing a training programme?
flashcard_questions.a: Facilities available and equipment available for training.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does a performer's age matter when designing a training programme?
flashcard_questions.a: Younger athletes have developing bones requiring careful loading; older athletes need more recovery time due to reduced elasticity.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the purpose of a warm-up before a training session?
flashcard_questions.a: It raises heart rate, increases blood flow to muscles, improves elasticity and reduces injury risk.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the purpose of a cool-down after a training session?
flashcard_questions.a: It gradually lowers heart rate, removes metabolic waste from muscles and aids recovery.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does lifestyle affect how a training programme is designed?
flashcard_questions.a: Diet, sleep, stress and work commitments affect recovery, so training load must fit the performer's real-life routine.

flashcard_questions.q: What should a coach do if a performer answers 'yes' to a PAR-Q question?
flashcard_questions.a: Seek medical clearance from a doctor before the performer starts training.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is it important to know a performer's current fitness level before writing their programme?
flashcard_questions.a: It establishes a baseline so training intensity is appropriate and progress can be measured over time.

flashcard_questions.q: How does knowing a sport's demands help a coach design a training programme?
flashcard_questions.a: It ensures the programme targets the fitness components most relevant to that sport's performance requirements.

glossary_terms.definition: Physical Activity Readiness Questionnaire — a short self-report health screening tool used to identify any medical conditions or risk factors that could make exercise unsafe.
A framework for setting goals that are Specific, Measurable, Agreed/Achievable, Realistic and Time-phased, ensuring they are clear, motivating and trackable.
The physical spaces, venues and equipment available to a performer that make certain types of training possible or restrict what can be included in a programme.
A structured preparatory phase at the start of a session that raises pulse and body temperature, improves muscle elasticity and prepares the performer mentally for exercise.
